items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The sum of the relative atomic masses of all the atoms in a formula"?
items.answer: relative formula mass (Mr)
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of relative formula mass (Mr).

items.stem: Distinguish between one mole of oxygen molecules and one mole of oxygen atoms.
items.answer: One mole of O atoms has a mass of 16 g; one mole of O₂ molecules contains twice as many atoms and has a mass of 32 g.
items.markingKey: One mole of O atoms has a mass of 16 g; one mole of O₂ molecules contains twice as many atoms and has a mass of 32 g. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why 12 g of carbon and 24 g of magnesium contain the same number of atoms.
items.answer: Each is one mole (Ar C = 12, Mg = 24), and one mole of any element contains 6.02 × 10²³ atoms.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Each is one mole (Ar C = 12, Mg = 24), and one mole of any element contains 6.02 × 10²³ atoms. (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Sofia plans to investigate how the number of moles of magnesium reacted affects the mass of magnesium oxide formed, to find the formula of magnesium oxide. State three variables that must be controlled to make this a fair test.
items.answer: Any three of: heating until constant mass; lid lifted only briefly; crucible cooled in a desiccator before weighing; clean ribbon (sandpapered)
items.markingKey: 1 mark each, max 3: heating until constant mass – all magnesium must react; lid lifted only briefly – prevents loss of MgO smoke; crucible cooled in a desiccator before weighing – hot crucibles give wrong mass readings; clean ribbon (sandpapered) – oxide coating adds mass. The independent or dependent variable scores 0.

items.stem: How many particles (formula units or molecules) are there in 92 g of C₂H₅OH (M = 46 g/mol)? (NA = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹)

Lars heated different masses of hydrated copper sulfate to constant mass and recorded the mass of water lost (three trials).

Mass of hydrated salt / g | Mass of water lost / g: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
1.0 | 0.38 | 0.37 | 0.38
2.0 | 0.76 | 0.74 | 0.72
3.0 | 1.13 | 1.11 | 1.10
4.0 | 1.50 | 1.55 | 1.50
5.0 | 1.90 | 1.87 | 1.95

Describe the trend shown by the results and explain it using scientific knowledge.
items.answer: The mass of water lost is directly proportional to the mass of hydrated copper sulfate heated. Hydrated copper sulfate (CuSO₄·5H₂O) contains a fixed ratio of 5 mol of water per mole of CuSO₄, so a fixed fraction (36%) of its mass is water.
items.markingKey: 1 trend: The mass of water lost is directly proportional to the mass of hydrated copper sulfate heated.; 1 use of data (quote means/values); 1-2 explanation: Hydrated copper sulfate (CuSO₄·5H₂O) contains a fixed ratio of 5 mol of water per mole of CuSO₄, so a fixed fraction (36%) of its mass is water.

items.stem: Priya investigated how the number of moles of magnesium reacted affects the mass of magnesium oxide formed, to find the formula of magnesium oxide. The method had this weakness: the crucible was weighed while still hot. Evaluate how this weakness affects the validity of the results and suggest an improvement to the method.
items.answer: cool it in a desiccator to room temperature before weighing
items.markingKey: 1 identifies how the weakness introduces error or an uncontrolled variable; 1 states the effect on the results/conclusion; 1-2 a specific, practical improvement: cool it in a desiccator to room temperature before weighing

items.stem: "The mole is too abstract to be taught before university." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: The mole is challenging but essential; with analogies and practice it is appropriate for MYP 5.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: the numbers are hard to imagine; students often confuse mass and moles. Arguments against: essential for quantitative chemistry, medicine doses, industry; analogies (a dozen, a ream) make it accessible. items.stem: What is the molar mass of water, H₂O (Ar: H = 1, O = 16)?
items.answer: 18 g/mol

items.stem: Explain why relative atomic masses are often not whole numbers.
items.answer: They are weighted averages of the masses of an element’s isotopes, e.g. chlorine is 75% ³⁵Cl and 25% ³⁷Cl, giving 35.5.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: They are weighted averages of the masses of an element’s isotopes, e.g. chlorine is 75% ³⁵Cl and 25% ³⁷Cl, giving 35.5. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims: "A mole is a unit of mass." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: The mole is the unit of amount of substance (number of particles); mass is in grams.
items.markingKey: The mole is the unit of amount of substance (number of particles); mass is in grams. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Using Redefining the kilogram and mole (2019) as an example, explain precision in measurement.
items.answer: The SI redefined the mole as exactly 6.022 140 76 × 10²³ particles, no longer tied to 12 g of carbon-12; silicon spheres with precisely counted atoms helped. Defining units by fixed constants makes them universal and stable.
items.markingKey: Context (The SI redefined the mole as exactly 6.022 140 76 × 10²³ particles, no longer tied to 12 g of carbon-12; silicon spheres with precisely counted atoms helped.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem: Explain what is meant by a mole and calculate (a) the number of moles in 22 g of CO₂, (b) the number of molecules, and (c) the number of oxygen atoms. (Ar: C = 12, O = 16; NA = 6.02 × 10²³)
items.answer: A mole is 6.02 × 10²³ particles. Mr CO₂ = 44; (a) 22 ÷ 44 = 0.5 mol; (b) 0.5 × 6.02 × 10²³ = 3.01 × 10²³ molecules; (c) 2 O per molecule → 6.02 × 10²³ O atoms.
items.markingKey: A mole is 6.02 × 10²³ particles. Mr CO₂ = 44; (a) 22 ÷ 44 = 0.5 mol; (b) 0.5 × 6.02 × 10²³ = 3.01 × 10²³ molecules; (c) 2 O per molecule → 6.02 × 10²³ O atoms.

items.stem: Define the term "excess reactant".
items.answer: The reactant that is left over when the reaction stops

items.stem: Freya writes: "In 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, 2 g of hydrogen reacts with 1 g of oxygen." Explain why this is inaccurate.

items.stem: Distinguish between the limiting reactant and the excess reactant.
items.answer: The limiting reactant is completely used and determines how much product forms; the excess reactant is left over.

items.stem:
Lukas added increasing masses of magnesium to 50 cm³ of 1.0 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid and measured the volume of hydrogen collected (three trials).

Mass of magnesium / g | Volume of hydrogen / cm³: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
0.1 | 105 | 105 | 105
0.2 | 219 | 219 | 213
0.4 | 430 | 413 | 416
0.6 | 627 | 630 | 622
0.8 | 653 | 660 | 622

Describe the trend shown by the results and explain it using scientific knowledge.
items.answer: The volume of hydrogen increases in proportion to the mass of magnesium up to 0.6 g, and then stays constant. Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂: at first magnesium is limiting; 50 cm³ of 1.0 mol/dm³ acid contains 0.05 mol HCl, which reacts with 0.025 mol (0.6 g) Mg, so above this the acid is limiting and no more hydrogen forms.
items.markingKey: 1 trend: The volume of hydrogen increases in proportion to the mass of magnesium up to 0.6 g, and then stays constant.; 1 use of data (quote means/values); 1-2 explanation: Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂: at first magnesium is limiting; 50 cm³ of 1.0 mol/dm³ acid contains 0.05 mol HCl, which reacts with 0.025 mol (0.6 g) Mg, so above this the acid is limiting and no more hydrogen forms.

items.answer: mass of solid residue (sodium carbonate) after heating to constant mass

items.markingKey: M1 moles of sodium = 23 ÷ 23 = 1 mol; M1 mole ratio 1 : 1 → 1 mol sodium chloride; A1 1 × 58.5 = 58.5 g.

items.stem: Iron is extracted by Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂. Calculate the mass of iron produced from 800 tonnes of iron(III) oxide, showing each step, and explain why the actual mass may be less. (Ar: Fe 56, O 16)
items.answer: Mr Fe₂O₃ = 160; 800 t = 800 × 10⁶ g ÷ 160 = 5 × 10⁶ mol; ratio 1 : 2 → 1 × 10⁷ mol Fe; × 56 = 5.6 × 10⁸ g = 560 t. Less in practice: impure ore, incomplete reaction, losses in handling, side reactions.
items.markingKey: Mr Fe₂O₃ = 160; 800 t = 800 × 10⁶ g ÷ 160 = 5 × 10⁶ mol; ratio 1 : 2 → 1 × 10⁷ mol Fe; × 56 = 5.6 × 10⁸ g = 560 t. Less in practice: impure ore, incomplete reaction, losses in handling, side reactions.

items.stem: Define the term "titration".
items.answer: A technique to find the exact volume of one solution that reacts with a known volume of another

items.stem: Explain why the conical flask is swirled during a titration.
items.answer: To mix the solutions thoroughly so the indicator shows the true end point.

items.stem: How many moles of acid are in 25 cm³ of 1 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid?

Omar titrated 25.0 cm³ portions of a hydrochloric acid solution diluted to different extents with 0.100 mol/dm³ sodium hydroxide (three titres each).

Acid concentration / mol/dm³ | Titre / cm³: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
0.04 | 11.08 | 11.05 | 10.94
0.08 | 23.53 | 21.84 | 23.16
0.12 | 33.00 | 35.08 | 33.49
0.16 | 44.14 | 43.72 | 43.93
0.2 | 57.71 | 54.66 | 56.40

State the acid concentration at which the repeat readings are least consistent, and calculate the range of the readings at that value. Suggest one way to make the data more reliable.
items.answer: 0.2 mol/dm³; range = 3.05 cm³; e.g. take more repeats and discard anomalies / use more precise apparatus
items.markingKey: 1 0.2 mol/dm³; 1 range = max − min = 57.71 − 54.66 = 3.05 cm³; 1 valid improvement (more repeats, more precise instrument, control a named variable).

items.stem:
Leila is investigating how the brand of vinegar affects its ethanoic acid concentration, found by titration with sodium hydroxide.
(a) State the independent variable. [1]
(b) State the dependent variable and how it will be measured. [1]
(c) Identify two control variables and explain why each must be kept constant. [2]
(d) Formulate a testable hypothesis and explain it using scientific reasoning. [2]
items.answer: (a) brand of vinegar (four brands, each diluted 1 : 10). (b) mean concordant titre of 0.100 mol/dm³ NaOH needed to neutralise 25.0 cm³ of diluted vinegar. (c) indicator and number of drops (phenolphthalein, 3) – end point judgement; dilution factor (1 : 10) using volumetric flask – concentration calculation depends on it. (d) If brand A is labelled 6% acidity, then it will need the largest titre, because a higher concentration of ethanoic acid needs more moles of NaOH to neutralise it.
items.markingKey: (a) 1: brand of vinegar (four brands, each diluted 1 : 10). (b) 1: mean concordant titre of 0.100 mol/dm³ NaOH needed to neutralise 25.0 cm³ of diluted vinegar (must include how/units). (c) 1 each, variable + reason: any two of volume of diluted vinegar (25.0 cm³ pipette) (more acid needs more alkali); concentration of NaOH (0.100 mol/dm³) (affects titre); indicator and number of drops (phenolphthalein, 3) (end point judgement); dilution factor (1 : 10) using volumetric flask (concentration calculation depends on it). (d) 1 for a testable if/then prediction linking IV and DV, 1 for correct scientific reasoning: If brand A is labelled 6% acidity, then it will need the largest titre, because a higher concentration of ethanoic acid needs more moles of NaOH to neutralise it.

items.stem: Describe how to carry out a titration to find the concentration of a sodium hydroxide solution using 0.100 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid, and show how the result would be calculated if the mean titre were 22.50 cm³ for 25.0 cm³ of alkali.
items.answer: Rinse and fill burette with acid; pipette 25.0 cm³ NaOH into conical flask; add 2–3 drops of phenolphthalein; titrate with swirling until pink just disappears; rough then accurate titres dropwise; repeat until concordant (±0.10 cm³). n(HCl) = 0.100 × 22.50/1000 = 2.25 × 10⁻³ mol; 1 : 1 ratio → n(NaOH) = 2.25 × 10⁻³; c = 2.25 × 10⁻³ ÷ 0.0250 = 0.0900 mol/dm³.
items.markingKey: Rinse and fill burette with acid; pipette 25.0 cm³ NaOH into conical flask; add 2–3 drops of phenolphthalein; titrate with swirling until pink just disappears; rough then accurate titres dropwise; repeat until concordant (±0.10 cm³). n(HCl) = 0.100 × 22.50/1000 = 2.25 × 10⁻³ mol; 1 : 1 ratio → n(NaOH) = 2.25 × 10⁻³; c = 2.25 × 10⁻³ ÷ 0.0250 = 0.0900 mol/dm³.

items.stem: "Titrations with a pH probe and data logger are better than using an indicator." Discuss.
items.answer: Data loggers give more information and objectivity, but indicators remain adequate for routine titrations.

Arguments against: probes must be calibrated and are more expensive; indicators are quick and reliable for simple acid–alkali titrations. Supported judgement: Data loggers give more information and objectivity, but indicators remain adequate for routine titrations. items.answer: mol/dm³ gives the number of moles per dm³; g/dm³ gives the mass per dm³; multiply mol/dm³ by molar mass to get g/dm³.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "atom economy"?

items.stem: Calcium carbonate decomposes: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂. 25 g of CaCO₃ is heated and 11.2 g of CaO is collected. Calculate the theoretical yield, the percentage yield, the volume of CO₂ at r.t.p. and the atom economy for CaO. (Mr CaCO₃ 100, CaO 56, CO₂ 44)

items.stem: A student claims: "A more concentrated solution always contains more solute." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: It contains more solute per dm³; a small volume of concentrated solution may contain less solute than a large volume of dilute solution.
items.markingKey: It contains more solute per dm³; a small volume of concentrated solution may contain less solute than a large volume of dilute solution. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: "One mole of a heavy gas takes up more space than one mole of a light gas." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: At the same temperature and pressure one mole of any gas occupies the same volume (24 dm³ at r.t.p.).
items.markingKey: At the same temperature and pressure one mole of any gas occupies the same volume (24 dm³ at r.t.p.). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A student claims: "One mole of every substance has the same mass." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: One mole contains the same number of particles, but the mass depends on the molar mass, e.g. 1 mol H₂ = 2 g, 1 mol CO₂ = 44 g.
items.markingKey: One mole contains the same number of particles, but the mass depends on the molar mass, e.g. 1 mol H₂ = 2 g, 1 mol CO₂ = 44 g. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂. Calculate the mass of iron formed from 160 g of iron(III) oxide. (M: iron(III) oxide 160 g/mol, iron 56 g/mol)
items.markingKey: M1 moles of iron(III) oxide = 160 ÷ 160 = 1 mol; M1 mole ratio 1 : 2 → 2 mol iron; A1 2 × 56 = 112 g.

items.stem:
Lukas titrated 25.0 cm³ portions of a hydrochloric acid solution diluted to different extents with 0.100 mol/dm³ sodium hydroxide (three titres each).

Acid concentration / mol/dm³ | Titre / cm³: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
0.04 | 9.03 | 9.64 | 9.38
0.08 | 19.10 | 19.45 | 18.89
0.12 | 28.39 | 28.61 | 27.84
0.16 | 37.49 | 36.78 | 37.11
0.2 | 47.16 | 47.86 | 47.18

State the acid concentration at which the repeat readings are least consistent, and calculate the range of the readings at that value. Suggest one way to make the data more reliable.
items.answer: 0.12 mol/dm³; range = 0.77 cm³; e.g. take more repeats and discard anomalies / use more precise apparatus
items.markingKey: 1 0.12 mol/dm³; 1 range = max − min = 28.61 − 27.84 = 0.77 cm³; 1 valid improvement (more repeats, more precise instrument, control a named variable).

items.stem: Aiko is investigating how the mass of magnesium reacting with excess acid affects the volume of hydrogen produced, to find the molar gas volume. Identify the independent variable in this investigation.
items.answer: mass of magnesium ribbon (0.02, 0.04, 0.06, 0.08, 0.10 g)
items.markingKey: 1 mark: mass of magnesium ribbon (0.02, 0.04, 0.06, 0.08, 0.10 g) (the variable that is deliberately changed). The measured variable scores 0.

items.stem: Jonas is investigating how the number of moles of magnesium reacted affects the mass of magnesium oxide formed, to find the formula of magnesium oxide. Formulate a testable hypothesis and justify it using scientific knowledge.
items.answer: If the moles of magnesium increase, then the moles of oxygen combined will increase in a 1 : 1 ratio, because the formula of magnesium oxide is MgO.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: testable prediction in "if … then …" form linking the independent and dependent variables; 1-2 marks: scientific explanation. Model: If the moles of magnesium increase, then the moles of oxygen combined will increase in a 1 : 1 ratio, because the formula of magnesium oxide is MgO.

items.stem:
Mei added increasing masses of magnesium to 50 cm³ of 1.0 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid and measured the volume of hydrogen collected (three trials).

Mass of magnesium / g | Volume of hydrogen / cm³: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
0.1 | 108 | 107 | 105
0.2 | 213 | 209 | 215
0.4 | 445 | 437 | 427
0.6 | 629 | 655 | 627
0.8 | 664 | 657 | 634

Describe the trend shown by the results and explain it using scientific knowledge.
items.answer: The volume of hydrogen increases in proportion to the mass of magnesium up to 0.6 g, and then stays constant. Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂: at first magnesium is limiting; 50 cm³ of 1.0 mol/dm³ acid contains 0.05 mol HCl, which reacts with 0.025 mol (0.6 g) Mg, so above this the acid is limiting and no more hydrogen forms.
items.markingKey: 1 trend: The volume of hydrogen increases in proportion to the mass of magnesium up to 0.6 g, and then stays constant.; 1 use of data (quote means/values); 1-2 explanation: Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂: at first magnesium is limiting; 50 cm³ of 1.0 mol/dm³ acid contains 0.05 mol HCl, which reacts with 0.025 mol (0.6 g) Mg, so above this the acid is limiting and no more hydrogen forms.

items.stem: Chloé is investigating how the brand of vinegar affects its ethanoic acid concentration, found by titration with sodium hydroxide. Identify the independent variable in this investigation.
items.answer: brand of vinegar (four brands, each diluted 1 : 10)
items.markingKey: 1 mark: brand of vinegar (four brands, each diluted 1 : 10) (the variable that is deliberately changed). The measured variable scores 0.

items.stem:
Maya made copper sulfate crystals using different heating times for the evaporation step and calculated the percentage yield (three batches each).

Evaporation time / min | Percentage yield / %: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
5 | 75 | 74 | 77
10 | 78 | 79 | 79
15 | 82 | 79 | 79
20 | 79 | 79 | 81
25 | 67 | 62 | 62

Calculate the percentage change in the mean percentage yield between 5 min and 25 min.
items.markingKey: M1 means 75.3 and 63.7; M1 (new − old) ÷ old × 100; A1 -15.5% (decrease).

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "The mole is too abstract to be taught before university."
items.answer: The mole is challenging but essential; with analogies and practice it is appropriate for MYP 5.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: the numbers are hard to imagine; students often confuse mass and moles. Arguments against: essential for quantitative chemistry, medicine doses, industry; analogies (a dozen, a ream) make it accessible. Supported judgement: The mole is challenging but essential; with analogies and practice it is appropriate for MYP 5.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "Atom economy is more important than yield when choosing an industrial process."
items.answer: Both matter; a sustainable process balances atom economy with yield, energy use and cost.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: high atom economy means less waste and fewer by-products; more sustainable. Arguments against: yield, rate, energy costs and safety also matter; by-products may be useful and sold. Supported judgement: Both matter; a sustainable process balances atom economy with yield, energy use and cost. Markbands (8 marks): MYP criterion D (0-8, scaled): 7-8 explains thoroughly how the science is applied to address the issue, discusses and evaluates the implications (moral, ethical, social, economic, political, cultural or environmental), and documents sources consistently; 5-6 explains and discusses; 3-4 outlines; 1-2 states.

items.stem: "Titrations with a pH probe and data logger are better than using an indicator." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Data loggers give more information and objectivity, but indicators remain adequate for routine titrations.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: no judgement of colour; works for coloured solutions; gives a full pH curve. Arguments against: probes must be calibrated and are more expensive; indicators are quick and reliable for simple acid–alkali titrations. Supported judgement: Data loggers give more information and objectivity, but indicators remain adequate for routine titrations. Markbands (8 marks): MYP criterion D (0-8, scaled): 7-8 explains thoroughly how the science is applied to address the issue, discusses and evaluates the implications (moral, ethical, social, economic, political, cultural or environmental), and documents sources consistently; 5-6 explains and discusses; 3-4 outlines; 1-2 states.

items.stem: Amara plans an investigation into how the mass of magnesium reacting with excess acid affects the volume of hydrogen produced, to find the molar gas volume. Describe how the results should be recorded, processed and presented, and explain how the reliability and validity of the conclusion will be judged.
items.answer: Results table with the independent variable (mass of magnesium ribbon (0.02, 0.04, 0.06, 0.08, 0.10 g)) in the first column and repeat readings of the dependent variable with units in headings; calculate means (ignoring anomalies); plot a suitable graph of the mean dependent variable against the independent variable with a line of best fit; describe the trend and compare with the hypothesis; judge reliability from the spread of repeats and validity from how well variables were controlled.
items.markingKey: 1 table with IV, repeats and units; 1 means calculated, anomalies identified and excluded; 1 appropriate graph (line graph/scatter for continuous IV, bar chart for categorical) with line of best fit; 1 trend compared with hypothesis; 1 reliability (spread of repeats) and validity (controls) discussed.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "Avogadro constant"?
options: Room temperature and pressure: about 20 °C and 1 atmosphere
6.02 × 10²³ per mole – the number of particles in one mole of a substance
A graduated tube with a tap used to add accurate, variable volumes in a titration
items.answer: 6.02 × 10²³ per mole – the number of particles in one mole of a substance
items.markingKey: B. "Avogadro constant" is 6.02 × 10²³ per mole – the number of particles in one mole of a substance.

items.stem: In N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃, how many moles of NH₃ form from 3 mol of H₂?
items.answer: 2 mol
items.markingKey: D. Ratio H₂ : NH₃ = 3 : 2.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The point in a titration when the indicator changes colour"?
items.answer: end point
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of end point.

items.stem: Explain the difference between theoretical yield and actual yield.
items.answer: Theoretical yield is calculated from the equation; actual yield is measured after the experiment and is usually less.
items.markingKey: Theoretical yield is calculated from the equation; actual yield is measured after the experiment and is usually less. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between relative formula mass and molar mass.
items.answer: Relative formula mass is a ratio with no units; molar mass has the same number but units of g/mol – the mass of one mole.
items.markingKey: Relative formula mass is a ratio with no units; molar mass has the same number but units of g/mol – the mass of one mole. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between a mass ratio and a mole ratio.
items.answer: A mass ratio compares grams; a mole ratio compares numbers of particles and comes directly from the balanced equation.
items.markingKey: A mass ratio compares grams; a mole ratio compares numbers of particles and comes directly from the balanced equation. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between concentration in g/dm³ and concentration in mol/dm³.
items.answer: mol/dm³ gives the number of moles per dm³; g/dm³ gives the mass per dm³; multiply mol/dm³ by molar mass to get g/dm³.
items.markingKey: mol/dm³ gives the number of moles per dm³; g/dm³ gives the mass per dm³; multiply mol/dm³ by molar mass to get g/dm³. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims: "A percentage yield above 100% means a very good experiment." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: A yield over 100% indicates an error, e.g. the product was still wet or impure.
items.markingKey: A yield over 100% indicates an error, e.g. the product was still wet or impure. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between molar mass and relative formula mass.
items.answer: Relative formula mass is a ratio with no units; molar mass has the same number but units of g/mol – the mass of one mole.
items.markingKey: Relative formula mass is a ratio with no units; molar mass has the same number but units of g/mol – the mass of one mole. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Jonas added increasing masses of magnesium to 50 cm³ of 1.0 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid and measured the volume of hydrogen collected (three trials).

Mass of magnesium / g | Volume of hydrogen / cm³: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
0.1 | 99 | 96 | 98
0.2 | 198 | 201 | 200
0.4 | 384 | 400 | 407
0.6 | 572 | 572 | 608
0.8 | 567 | 578 | 567

Calculate the mean volume of hydrogen when the mass of magnesium was 0.6 g.
items.markingKey: M1 (572 + 572 + 608) ÷ 3; A1 584.0 cm³ (unit and sensible precision).

items.stem: In an investigation into how the brand of vinegar affects its ethanoic acid concentration, found by titration with sodium hydroxide, explain why this control must be applied in the same way in every trial: dilution factor (1 : 10) using volumetric flask.
items.answer: concentration calculation depends on it
items.markingKey: 1 mark: a change in this variable (dilution factor (1 : 10) using volumetric flask) would also affect the dependent variable; 1 mark for the specific reason: concentration calculation depends on it. Then only the independent variable is responsible for any change (validity).

items.stem: A reaction produced 480 cm³ of hydrogen at r.t.p. How many moles is this?
items.answer: 0.02 mol

items.stem: Calculate the molar mass of Mg. (Ar: H 1, C 12, N 14, O 16, Na 23, Mg 24, S 32, Cl 35.5, K 39, Ca 40, Fe 56, Cu 63.5)
items.answer: 24 g/mol
items.markingKey: M1 24; A1 24 g/mol.

items.stem: Maya wants to find out how the mass of sodium hydrogencarbonate heated affects the mass of sodium carbonate produced, to test the equation 2NaHCO₃ → Na₂CO₃ + H₂O + CO₂. Write a focused research question for this investigation that names both the independent and the dependent variable.
items.answer: How does mass of sodium hydrogencarbonate affect mass of solid residue?
items.markingKey: 1 mark: names the independent variable (mass of sodium hydrogencarbonate (1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0 g)); 1 mark: names the measurable dependent variable (mass of solid residue (sodium carbonate) after heating to constant mass) in a question form.

items.stem: 0.2 mol of sodium hydroxide is dissolved to make 200 cm³ of solution. Calculate the concentration in mol/dm³.
items.answer: 1 mol/dm³
items.markingKey: M1 V = 200 ÷ 1000 = 0.2 dm³; M1 c = n ÷ V; A1 1 mol/dm³.

items.stem: In an investigation into how the mass of magnesium reacting with excess acid affects the volume of hydrogen produced, to find the molar gas volume, explain why this control must be applied in the same way in every trial: excess acid (50 cm³ of 1.0 mol/dm³ HCl).
items.answer: magnesium must be the limiting reactant
items.markingKey: 1 mark: a change in this variable (excess acid (50 cm³ of 1.0 mol/dm³ HCl)) would also affect the dependent variable; 1 mark for the specific reason: magnesium must be the limiting reactant. Then only the independent variable is responsible for any change (validity).

items.stem: Design a safe and valid method to investigate how the brand of vinegar affects its ethanoic acid concentration, found by titration with sodium hydroxide. In your answer include the variables, the equipment, the range and number of values of the independent variable, the number of repeats, safety and how the data will be recorded and processed.
items.answer: Dilute 25.0 cm³ of each vinegar to 250 cm³ in a volumetric flask; pipette 25.0 cm³ into a conical flask; add phenolphthalein; titrate with NaOH from a burette until a permanent pale pink; repeat until concordant; calculate concentration (×10 for dilution) and compare with labels.
items.markingKey: MYP criterion B: 1 independent variable with at least 5 values in a sensible range; 1 dependent variable and how it is measured; 1 at least two controls and how they are controlled; 1 logical step-by-step procedure with equipment; 1 at least 3 repeats and calculation of a mean; 1 relevant safety point (sodium hydroxide is corrosive – wear eye protection; use a pipette filler, never mouth-pipette). Model: Dilute 25.0 cm³ of each vinegar to 250 cm³ in a volumetric flask; pipette 25.0 cm³ into a conical flask; add phenolphthalein; titrate with NaOH from a burette until a permanent pale pink; repeat until concordant; calculate concentration (×10 for dilution) and compare with labels.

items.stem: "Chemical companies should be required to choose the process with the highest atom economy." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Atom economy should be a major factor, but decisions need to balance it with yield, energy and safety.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: less waste, more sustainable use of resources. Arguments against: other factors – yield, rate, energy use, safety and cost – may make a lower atom economy route better; by-products may be useful. Supported judgement: Atom economy should be a major factor, but decisions need to balance it with yield, energy and safety.
